limitations: DRC proves only that this exact PCB passed the configured KiCad physical design rules.
DRC does not prove functional correctness, signal integrity, thermal or EMC performance, RF behavior, universal manufacturability, firmware behavior, or hardware operation.
A zero-violation ERC result establishes only that this exact generated schematic passed the configured KiCad electrical checks.
ERC does not establish functional or datasheet correctness, simulation behavior, PCB layout, manufacturability, firmware behavior, or hardware performance.
PB-I2C-002: Pull-up resistance is range-checked against common practice, not calculated from bus capacitance and rise time. Actual rise time stays NOT_VERIFIED until layout is known.

PB-LED-001: The driving pin's own current rating is not checked: the catalog does not record per-pin source and sink limits, so an LED within its own rating could still exceed what the GPIO driving it can supply.

PB-PWR-004: Presence only. A netlist cannot show that a capacitor is physically close to the pin it decouples, and placement is what makes decoupling work. Capacitor placement stays NOT_VERIFIED until board layout is reviewed.
PB-PWR-004: Capacitors are counted per rail net, not attributed to individual supply pins. A part with several supply pins on one net may pass here while still lacking a capacitor at each pin.

PB-REG-002: Load is summed from published maxima, which are worst-case figures that rarely occur simultaneously. This is deliberately conservative and is not a thermal analysis: package power dissipation and rise above ambient are NOT_VERIFIED.
PB-UART-001: Orientation against an external programmer cannot be verified from connectivity. Where a UART reaches a bare header, the wiring stays HUMAN_CONFIRMED at best.

flows.basis: declared external source, regulator power-out pins, and net membership
flows.label: Power
flows.question: Where does the electricity go?

stages.detail: The USB power connector brings 5 V from USB into the board.
stages.title: Power arrives

stages.detail: The 3.3 V voltage regulator takes that in and produces a steadier, lower 3.3 V power. Turning one voltage into another is the whole job of a voltage regulator.
stages.title: The regulator steps it down

stages.detail: The programming header, main computer and sensor all take their supply from that 3.3 V power.
stages.title: Everything else runs from it

flows.summary: 5 V from USB comes in from the connector, the 3.3 V voltage regulator converts it, and 3.3 V power feeds the rest of the board.

flows.basis: peripheral-side bus pin names, then net membership
flows.label: Sensor data
flows.question: How does a measurement reach the processor?

stages.detail: The included sensors provide measurements that a program can request.
stages.title: The sensors measure

stages.detail: Two wires run between them: one carries the data, the other a clock so both ends agree when each bit is valid.
stages.title: Two wires carry data

stages.detail: A resistor on each wire holds them up when nothing is driving them. Without that they would float at an undefined level and the reading would be unreliable.
stages.title: Resistors hold the wires high

stages.detail: The 4.7 kohm pull-up resistor and main computer receives the measurement.
stages.title: The processor reads it

flows.summary: The sensor talks to the 4.7 kohm pull-up resistor and main computer over two shared wires.

flows.basis: switch categories, connected signal/ground nets and observed supply pull-ups
flows.label: Button inputs
flows.question: How does a press become an input?

stages.detail: The included pull-up resistors bias the inputs toward their supply when the buttons are open.
stages.title: Give the idle input a level

stages.detail: These buttons connect their signal to ground when their contacts close.
stages.title: Close the button contacts

stages.detail: Firmware must configure and read the input, filter contact bounce, and choose a response. Wiring a button does not supply that program.
stages.title: Let the program interpret the press

flows.summary: A button changes an electrical connection. A program reads its input pin and decides what should happen; no button behavior is simulated here.

flows.label: Light 1
flows.question: How does the board show me something?

stages.detail: The main computer turns the indicator on and off with one output pin when firmware drives it.
stages.title: The processor switches a pin

stages.detail: The 330 ohm current-limiting resistor sits in line with the light. It limits current; excessive current can damage an LED.
stages.title: A resistor limits the current

stages.detail: Current flows through the light to ground, and it glows.
stages.title: The LED lights

flows.summary: A program can use one processor pin to switch the indicator light on and off through the 330 ohm current-limiting resistor.
